articles.title: Pyrograzing turns ordinary livestock into fire prevention heroes, so why isn’t it used on public lands more often?
articles.author:
<name>Briana Swette, Social-Ecological Systems Scientist, Boise State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/briana-swette-2744195"/>
paras: In grasslands across the American West, four-legged fire prevention crews are busy at work, helping keep wildfire risk under control. These cattle, goats and sheep stomp down tall grasses as they munch their way through plants that could otherwise burn, lowering the risk of catastrophic fires in the process.

When livestock are intentionally used for wildfire control like this, the practice is known as targeted grazing. And it’s gaining attention as severe wildfire seasons push firefighters and public land budgets to the brink .

Strategically removing trees, shrubs and grasses can help alter the trajectory of future wildfires , but it is complex and expensive work that often involves intentional burning, herbicides and heavy machinery to thin forests or create fuel breaks.
Livestock can do some of this work instead, simply by grazing in the right places.

Current leaders of the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management are pushing for more targeted grazing in National Forests and on other public lands as part of the 2025 Grazing Action Plan and its accompanying directives .
As rangeland scientists who study how to effectively use livestock grazing to manage wildfire fuels and invasive plants, we see potential but also limitations to this strategy.
Targeted pyrograzing can help manage wildfire risk well in certain contexts .

Livestock do not eat or trample large, woody trees, but most wildfires burn in grass and shrublands that livestock can help maintain. Beef cattle, for example, consumed around 600 pounds of vegetation per acre across nearly 34 million acres in California alone in 2017. In places such as Santa Clara County, California, grazing is now a formal part of wildfire management plans.
The goal is not necessarily to prevent wildfire altogether but to reduce flammable vegetation enough to avoid fueling catastrophic wildfires.

Removing hazardous fuels through livestock grazing and trampling can help slow a fire’s spread so firefighters can stop the fire before it enters communities or reduce its intensity so ecosystems are able to rebound afterward.
In some cases, grazing can be more practical or cost-effective than other fire risk reduction methods.

For example, intentional burning is dangerous where there is so much vegetation that fires would burn too hot and fast to control. In other places, it isn’t feasible to spray herbicides across large areas or bring in heavy equipment to clear vegetation in remote locations.
But goats, sheep and cattle can eat their way across remote or steep terrain with little trouble.

We’ve spoken with savvy land managers who are also using livestock grazing to remove vegetation before carrying out intentional burns to make conditions safer for those fires . We’ve heard from others who are planning to use grazing before spraying herbicide to treat flammable invasive grasses to make it more effective.

A quarter of the U.S. Forest Service’s ranger districts in the Pacific Northwest, Intermountain and Pacific Southwest have used some kind of targeted grazing to manage fire risk. When we surveyed over 1,000 U.S. Forest Service staff, we found a majority think targeted grazing can be at least moderately effective to help with wildfire risk management, and over two-thirds rated past projects as moderately to extremely effective .
Using targeted grazing at the scale needed to address widespread wildfire risk across federal lands would be difficult, and it won’t work everywhere.

To effectively reduce wildfire fuel with grazing, ranchers often need to bring livestock to certain areas at different times of year than usual, haul water so livestock can work in areas without natural water sources, or keep livestock in areas for longer than would be ideal for their weight gain.

Those factors cost ranchers money and can require shifts in their operation that aren’t practical. Or in certain contexts, animals simply may be unable to graze enough to achieve the desired reduction in wildfire risk.

Just 5% of Forest Service staff in the survey we conducted in 2025 reported that they were very likely or extremely likely to use targeted grazing in the next few years. Their answers were driven by how effective they believed targeted grazing could be, but also whether they felt they would have time to plan and manage it.

In particular, we found they were concerned about a lack of monitoring to ensure projects have the intended effect. Their ratings were also strongly connected to whether they felt that ranchers who already graze livestock on public lands could actually implement targeted grazing. And very few staff thought it would be feasible for the agency to pay ranchers to conduct targeted grazing as a vegetation treatment.

As the Grazing Action Plan pushes federal agencies to expand the use of targeted grazing, work is underway to evaluate where it could be effective. Some uncertainties remain, including around the question of paying ranchers and herders to perform targeted grazing as the practice scales up. Environmental groups have also sued over the plan , arguing that it would put wildlife at risk and is simply an excuse to open more land for ranchers.
While grazing is not appropriate everywhere, our research finds good examples of U.S. Forest Service staff incorporating livestock grazing into fire and fuels planning .

In Idaho, we are working with ranchers to test using sheep to reduce highly flammable and invasive grasses. In some years, the sheep have substantially reduced the amount of flammable invasive grass and even boosted the cover of native wildflowers. They have reduced invasive grass cover by over 20% in some years. Other times, the invasive grass matures so early that it is difficult to get the sheep to the target areas at the right time.

Overall, we have experienced firsthand the value when ranchers, herders, agency staff and scientists work together toward shared environmental goals. We believe the U.S. would benefit from financial and technical investment in both agency staff and ranchers to plan and perform targeted grazing so the practice can become a tried-and-true part of America’s strategy to live with wildfire.

articles.title: Wyze treats home security like a social feed with new AI-powered ‘Stories’ feature
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Smart home device maker Wyze wants to end notification fatigue by turning security footage into something more akin to an Instagram feed.
The Kirkland, Wash.-based company launched “Wyze Stories,” a new AI-powered feature that stitches together clip sequences from multiple cameras into a single, chronological event.

Instead of firing off separate alerts as a visitor moves from the driveway to the front porch, the system uses multi-camera grouping and event importance filtering to deliver a unified highlight reel alongside a descriptive, text-based summary.

“Honestly, the number one thing people complain about with security cameras is getting blown up with notifications,” Dave Crosby, co-founder and chief marketing officer at Wyze, said in a news release Tuesday. “Instead of digging through a mess of clips, you just tap through daily stories like your house is your favorite social feed.”

Within the app, stories are indicated by glowing green-and-purple rings on the home tab, allowing users to tap through footage, hold to pause, or watch events at double speed. The feature also uses AI to generate instant written summaries of detected activity — such as noting when a delivery driver leaves a box at the door — and automatically highlights high-importance events while suppressing repetitive, minor alerts.

The new feature is available as part of Wyze’s top-tier “Cam Unlimited Pro” subscription, which costs $19.99 a month and includes features like cross-camera grouping, 24/7 emergency dispatch, and 60 days of cloud storage.
Wyze Stories works across most of the company’s hardware lineup, with the exception of older legacy models like the original Wyze Cam, Doorbell v1, and Outdoor v1 and v2.

Founded in 2017 by a trio of former Amazon employees, Wyze originally launched with a $20 smart camera before expanding into a broader lineup of sensors, lighting, and home security systems. The company raised $110 million in 2021 and ranks No. 20 on the GeekWire 200 index of top Pacific Northwest startups.

articles.title: Madrona’s annual IA40 list shows an AI industry splitting in two
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Seattle-based venture capital firm Madrona released its sixth annual Intelligent Applications 40 list this week, naming 45 private AI companies (the five extras come from ties) that have collectively raised $410 billion from investors across the industry.
Three of them — Anthropic, OpenAI and Databricks — account for 92% of that total.

The uneven distribution of funding reflects a larger split in the tech industry, as the largest AI companies make huge bets on the computing capacity needed to meet demand for their models, while almost everyone else builds businesses on top of them.

The frontier labs are “increasingly funded by strategic capital from the likes of Amazon, Google, Nvidia and SoftBank rather than traditional venture,” Madrona’s Matt McIlwain and Rolanda Fu wrote in a post accompanying the list . That scale, they added, “makes every other category on this list look capital light by comparison.”
On top of that, he said, hundreds of billions of dollars are flowing into OpenAI and Anthropic.

“And what I say to both the big tech companies and to the people funding the model companies: thank you very much,” McIlwain said on Bloomberg TV , noting that the five largest tech companies will spend an estimated $750 billion in capital expenditures this year.

But even setting those big three aside, McIlwain said, the rest of the winners have raised an average of more than $800 million each. That’s a total of $34 billion combined. Companies across the list are raising far more than they used to, enough that Madrona had to redraw its own categories.

The list sorts companies by total capital raised, and this year the ceiling for “early stage” rose to $50 million, up from the $30 million threshold that held for the previous five lists. The cutoff for “emerging enablers,” its category for smaller infrastructure companies, doubled to $100 million.
“Companies across the board are raising more money, and the definition for what ‘early’ means continues to shift higher,” McIlwain and Fu wrote.

Madrona has published the IA40 since 2021 as a roster of the private companies it considers most important in building and enabling AI applications. According to the firm, this year’s list drew on input from 72 investors representing 54 venture and corporate firms, who nominated and voted on more than 450 companies, with PitchBook data factored into the scoring.
Two Seattle-area companies made this year’s list:
Last year’s list included two other Seattle-area companies in addition to Clarify.

Madrona, one of the Seattle region’s largest and oldest venture capital firms, is an investor in all four — Clarify, Gradial, Statsig and Dropzone AI — although it also invests outside the region, and many of the companies on the IA40 are not in its portfolio.

Several of the companies on this year’s list have engineering centers in the Seattle region , including Anthropic, which leased 113,000 square feet in South Lake Union this year; OpenAI, which expanded to nearly 300,000 square feet in downtown Bellevue after the Statsig acquisition; and Anduril, which employs about 560 people in Bellevue and Seattle.

Databricks, the San Francisco-based data and AI company (which leased 142,000 square feet in Bellevue this year), is the only company to appear on all six IA40 lists. That said, 23 of last year’s 40 winners returned this year, a 58% repeat rate, up from 33% the year before.

McIlwain and Fu wrote that the biggest and most established companies on the list are holding their spots, noting that “the age of experimentation is giving way to an age of enterprise readiness,” with buyers and investors “paying premiums for companies that can demonstrate real ROI.”
Madrona will recognize the winners at its IA40 Summit in Seattle on Sept. 29 and 30.
Updated with Matt McIlwain’s comments to Bloomberg TV.

articles.title: Juno Propulsion wins $1.2M grant from NSF to advance non-toxic space propulsion system
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: The National Science Foundation has awarded a $1.2 million grant to Tukwila, Wash.-based Juno Propulsion to support the startup’s development of a non-toxic propulsion system for in-space applications.

The two-year Phase II project, funded through NSF’s Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, will be conducted in partnership with the University of Washington and UW Professor Carl Knowlen’s lab. The focus of the funding is to support work on Juno’s Product Development Unit (PDU), which uses rotating detonation rocket engine technology .

By combining high-efficiency propulsion with non-toxic propellants, Juno aims to enable spacecraft to maneuver farther and faster while reducing the risks associated with traditional toxic propellants. Work on the PDU is intended to advance Juno’s system to Technology Readiness Level 8, positioning it near production-ready status on the standard 1-to-9 TRL scale .

“This award represents an important milestone in taking our rotating detonation propulsion technology from development and flight demonstration toward a production-ready product,” Juno Propulsion CEO Alexis Harroun said in a news release. “We’re excited to continue our collaboration with the University of Washington and Professor Knowlen’s lab as we take the next step toward delivering this technology to commercial and government customers.”
The Phase II grant, announced last week, follows up on a $275,000 Phase I SBIR grant that was awarded in 2024.

Juno Propulsion’s team is getting ready for Project Iris , an on-orbit demonstration of its propulsion technology that’s due to fly aboard Momentus’ Vigoride 8 satellite platform in 2027. The lessons learned from Project Iris will feed directly into work on the PDU.

The startup was founded in 2023 by Harroun and chief technology officer Ari Martinez , who met while earning their Ph.D.s at Purdue University. Harroun received her undergraduate degree in aeronautics and astronautics from UW and interned at Blue Origin, Boeing and NASA before heading to Purdue.

In June, Juno Propulsion announced the close of a $1.4 million pre-seed financing round , led by SOSV with participation from Hypernova Fund, Leslie Ventures, Activate, Collaborative Fund, Safar Partners and Cape Fear Ventures.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Seattle Press Are Concocting a False Narrative to Undermine Mayor Wilson
articles.author: Maggie Block
paras: I am losing my mind consuming the local news coverage of the Seattle Center shooting and its aftermath.

I want to be clear right at the top, that I believe the job of the media, of journalism, is to hold those in power accountable. And if local broadcast and legacy media want to focus on holding our progressive city leaders to account, on legitimate concerns – crucially, in a way balanced with how they cover business-focused “moderate” politicians – I will welcome them with open arms.
But KIRO and KOMO’s coverage of Mayor Katie Wilson’s office in general, and after the Bite of Seattle shooting in particular, is something they need to be held accountable for.

On Monday, KIRO's newly installed news director, Jennifer Dahl, sat on a panel at Scenius Social billed as a conversation about art and Seattle's creative community. Twice, she turned the conversation toward Mayor Wilson and the communication failure after the Seattle Center shooting, a failure the mayor has already admitted.
Dahl warned that it could "happen again," invoking a mass shooting in Oregon.
Nothing sharpens a narrative quite like fear.
And I’m loath to admit it, but the failure was real.
However, Wilson has apologized. She asked the city's independent Inspector General to reconstruct what happened, figure out why it happened, and recommend how to prevent it from happening again.

I know that is something we rarely see from political leaders, so I can understand why a lay person may not know how to identify it. But professional journalists should know: that’s what accountability looks like.
Accountability is not turning one mistake into an albatross and hanging it around a woman's neck until Election Day.
Three people died at Seattle Center. A two-year-old was wounded. Families are grieving. Workers who tried to save lives are carrying images I imagine they would give anything to forget.
And somehow the great political question emerging from all of this has become: Why wasn't the mayor standing behind a microphone sooner?

Had the press conference happened exactly on time, three people would still be dead. The failure was in communicating about the response, not the response itself. Those are different things. Turning them into the same thing is not journalism happening naturally. It is an editorial choice. Then Dahl suggested the city should "turn on the Flock cameras."

Except, Seattle doesn't have Flock cameras . It has CCTV operated by the vendor Axon . Further, I am confused as to what Dahl imagines surveillance cameras could have done, as there were police officers standing roughly four paces from the shooters at Bite of Seattle.
How could a camera have stopped what armed police officers standing feet away could not?
This is how consent gets manufactured. Not through some smoky-room conspiracy where editors decide what you're allowed to believe. It's much more ordinary than that.

They decide what matters. Three people are killed, and yet the delayed press conference becomes the story. A delay of a few hours, confusion, questions about who was in charge, repeated again and again, until a single detail hardens into a verdict: City Hall is dysfunctional.

After that, the story begins feeding itself. A disagreement between SPD and the mayor becomes more evidence. A few councilmembers sharply criticize her and now there are "growing questions about her leadership." Then somebody commissions a poll asking voters whether they're worried about her leadership, and suddenly the media is reporting a public perception it helped manufacture.
Every individual fact can be true while the story constructed from them is bullshit.
Because a mayor arriving late to a podium is television.

The slow, boring, desperately important work of preventing the next shooting, youth programs, housing, coordination, intervention, mental health care, and the unglamorous labor of keeping people alive, isn't.
Our housing crisis did not begin in January. Homelessness did not begin in January. Public safety problems did not begin in January. Neither did government communication failures.

I remember 2020, after Lorenzo Anderson was shot during CHOP, when Seattle Fire waited nearby while police and fire struggled to coordinate their response. Mayor Jenny Durkan privately called what happened "foreseeable and avoidable" and ordered her chiefs to make sure it didn't happen again.
I don't mention that to excuse Wilson's mistake. Trust me, I have plenty of criticisms of my own for Seattle’s mayor. I mention it because history did not begin the morning Katie Wilson became mayor.
If communication breakdowns after deadly violence happened under previous administrations, then somebody should explain why this failure proves something uniquely rotten about this one.
Otherwise we're not applying a standard, but constructing one.
If one listens to local news lately and you'd think somebody handed Katie Wilson the keys to a perfectly functioning Seattle and she totaled it pulling out of the parking lot.

Take Starbucks. Recent coverage has asked whether layoffs at the company prove Seattle has become hostile to business. Except Starbucks cut roughly 2,000 corporate jobs across two rounds in 2025, before Wilson was mayor, as part of a turnaround strategy that began the previous September and sought billions in cost reductions.
That is a multinational corporation following its own restructuring plan.
It is not eight months of Katie Wilson's mayoralty somehow reaching backward through time.
Since we're suddenly so worried about Seattle's "business climate," when exactly do we get a nightly segment about the climate for workers?

You know, the people wondering whether they can pay rent. Buy groceries. Afford childcare. Keep living in the city where they work. Why does their anxiety always seem to be less newsworthy than a shareholder's?

The same thing happened with the recall petition filed by a married couple who also happened to have voted for her opponent last November. Every responsible outlet acknowledged it has little chance of surviving judicial review. In fact, the couple rescinded their recall filing this week, as the effort ran into the buzzsaw of a skeptical judge at its first hearing. But politically, it doesn't have to survive. It just has to consume oxygen.

That's how a housing affordability press conference becomes a press conference about the recall, while universal school meals , junk-fee protections and restrictions on surveillance-based dynamic grocery pricing struggle for the same attention.

Councilmember Bob Kettle held his own public safety press conference just before the mayor signed a set of executive orders accelerating Vision Zero . Seattle had 27 traffic deaths in 2025, including 18 pedestrians, compared with 37 homicides. Different causes. Similar human stakes.
Yet one produces weeks of breathless coverage while the other mostly produces passing mention and sad little roadside memorials we drive past on the way to work. Why?

That makes her human. It does not automatically make her uniquely incompetent. There has never been a flawless executive leader, anywhere. Certainly not in Seattle. And I have never seen the broadcast news concoct such a grandiose story around mayoral incompetence, despite far more deserving examples.
So it’s time to start asking questions of the people asking the questions.
Why does the business owner get the microphone while the worker disappears?
Why is the person demanding more cameras treated as an authority on safety while the person who will be watched by those cameras gets called an activist?

articles.title: The Ultimate ORCA Speedrun
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: At 9:59am last Friday, I boarded Everett Transit Route 29 at Everett Transit Mall Station. While the six other passengers on the bus were traveling to work, home, or somewhere else, for me this trip was the first segment of my region-wide ORCA speedrun. Transit speedrunning is the process of visiting every station in a transit system as fast as possible. In cities/regions with complex rail transit networks, such as San Francisco or New York , competitors look for new routes to beat the previous record. While the Link light rail system now has 3 lines across Puget Sound, the speedrun route is fairly straightforward . Our rail network is not complex enough to provide other potential routes that are faster. However, the broader ORCA network is quite complex.

One Regional Card for All (ORCA) powers transit fares for nine transit agencies across four counties in Washington. Visiting every stop in the ORCA network would take months, so the ORCA speedrun has a simpler goal: ride every mode of fixed-route transit offered by each agency in the ORCA pod, as fast as possible. This includes every type bus service, rail service, and ferry service from each of the nine agencies. For example, King County Metro offers three types of bus service: local, express, and RapidRide. Likewise, Kitsap Transit has both Fast Ferries and Foot Ferries. In total, there are 21 different modes across the nine agencies. Paratransit, dial-a-ride-transit, or other on-demand services are not included. City Beautiful and The Transit Bandit have completed similar speedruns using seven of the transit modes in Seattle.

Centered around downtown Seattle, ORCA is supported by agencies to the north, south, and west. For my speedrun, I started in the north (Everett) and planned to finish in the south (Tacoma). I shared updates in real-time on Bluesky and a full map of the run is available here .

Snohomish County has two dedicated transit agencies: Everett Transit (ET) and Community Transit (CT). ET is one of the smaller agencies on the list, it just runs local bus service. CT, meanwhile, has local bus routes, Express bus routes and Swift routes.

My trip on Route 29 checked the Everett Transit box. I got off the bus at the South Everett Freeway Station and transferred to an inbound Community Transit Express Route 905. Route 905 returned to I-5 and traveled directly to Lynnwood Transit Center. As I would need to return back to Lynnwood TC to board Link to get to Seattle, this next segment required an out-and-back using both Swift and a local route. I boarded the next Orange Line bus towards Edmonds College and took it one stop to Hwy 99. Thankfully, the traffic signal at Hwy 99 & 196th St was in my favor so I could catch the Lynnwood-bound Route 166 across the street with seconds to spare.

Link is the best option for traveling between Lynnwood and Seattle. The 40 minute ride was a nice opportunity to relax after a few very close transfers in Snohomish County. In Seattle, I had about an hour to ride five different modes: Metro bus, Metro Express bus, Seattle Streetcar, ST Express bus, and the Seattle Center Monorail. While I had planned most of the day, this hour was improvised. At Westlake station, I got off the 1 Line and walked over to the waiting South Lake Union streetcar. I hopped aboard and we departed a few minutes later. After two stops, I alighted the streetcar at Denny Way and boarded an eastbound Route 8 bus. As we sped down the new bus lane on Denny, I noticed a ST Express Route 577 bus was about to start its trip to Federal Way. I got off Route 8 after just one stop and ran to the bus stop at Boren Ave & Virginia St. The Route 577 bus arrived a few moments later, exactly on time.

I now had just two modes left for downtown Seattle: the Seattle Center Monorail and a Metro Express bus. Most Metro Express buses run during peak hours so my only option was Route 28X. I rode Route 577 a few stops to Stewart St & 7th Ave. After a short walk to Westlake Center Mall, I boarded a well timed monorail train and made my way to Seattle Center. I sat near the front of the train as I needed to make a quick exit to catch the next bus. A southbound Route 28X bus was scheduled to depart from 7th & Thomas at 11:52am, four minutes after the monorail arrived at Seattle Center. A four minute transfer is usually fine, but this bus stop was a 7 minute walk from the monorail station.

After a short jog I made it to the bus stop 2 minutes early (the bus was 1 minute late). I boarded the 28X bus to check off the last mode needed in downtown Seattle. My next scheduled ride was the 12:30pm West Seattle Water Taxi operated by King County Metro. With 25 minutes to spare I decided to ride Metro’s Waterfront Shuttle.

I arrived back at Pier 50 at 12:19 and joined the queue to board my first boat of the day. Metro’s West Seattle Water Taxi took just 10 minutes to reach Seacrest Dock. I boarded on DART Route 773 for a quick ride to Avalon Ave & Bradford, just south of the West Seattle Bridge. After crossing the street, I caught an inbound C Line bus back to downtown Seattle. This RapidRide bus was the fourth and final mode of the day from King County Metro.

The C Line bus sailed across the West Seattle Bridge and dropped me off across the street from the Seattle Ferry Terminal. After enjoying some of the ferry terminal amenities, we (my wife joined me for this section) boarded the Seattle – Bremerton Washington State Ferries route. The hour-long trip sailed by and we arrived in Bremerton at 2:39pm, just 9 minutes behind schedule. Despite the delay we had a few minutes for a delicious lunch at Mezcalitos. At 3:30p, we walked back over to the ferry terminal to catch the smallest boat of the day: a Kitsap Transit Foot Ferry to Annapolis. The Admiral Pete was packed to standing-room-only as we made the short trip to Annapolis. We alighted the vessel with everyone else and started to walk down the surprisingly long dock. When we were halfway to land, the boat’s engines roared to life and it sailed away. This was not the plan. We were supposed to take that same boat back to Bremerton. The 15-minute wait for the next sailing put the most important transfer of the day in jeopardy.

The next boat back to Bremerton was scheduled to get us back to Bremerton at 4:07pm. That would leave just four minutes to catch the 4:11pm Worker/Driver bus from the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard (PSNS). Worker/Driver buses run just once per day in each direction, so missing it would end this speed run attempt. After enjoying a private boat experience on the Foot Ferry trip back to Bremerton, I left the backpack with my wife and sprinted to PSNS. About a minute later, the retractable bollards descended and the Route 613 (Chico) bus rolled through the gate.

Kitsap Transit’s Worker/Driver routes are unique in Puget Sound. They travel from across Kitsap County to downtown Bremerton and PSNS. While they are designed for PSNS employees (and only PSNS employees can ride them within the facility), their one stop outside the PSNS gate makes them available to the public. I did confirm that these routes are open to the public with Kitsap Transit staff a few weeks ago. As the Worker/Driver routes travel long distances, they have far stop spacing. I rode Route 631 one stop (2.5 miles), to Kitsap Way & Marine Dr. Here, I had a lofty 10 minute transfer to Kitsap Route 212 back to the ferry terminal.

As luck would have it, Route 212 was running 17 minutes behind schedule and was scheduled to arrive at the Bremerton Terminal at 4:57pm. I needed to catch the 5:00pm Fast Ferry back to Seattle. As the Fast Ferry requires all passengers to be on board 2 minutes before departure, this would cut it way to close. Fortunately, there was a Route 226 bus from the same stop that was scheduled to arrive at the terminal at 4:55pm. Still too close for comfort, but I didn’t have another option. Route 226 arrived on time and I was finally heading back to the ferry terminal. While on board, I noticed the Route 226 had a slight detour in downtown Bremerton. Still worried about catching the Fast Ferry, I decided to get off the bus at Pacific and MLK Way and run the rest of the way. I met back up with my wife and we joined the line to board the Fast Ferry at 4:56pm.

The Fast Ferry was busy! Nearly every seat was occupied as we made the 30-minute trip back to Seattle. We got off the boat at 5:33pm, leaving just 12 minutes to catch the 5:45pm Sounder train to Tacoma. After saying goodbye to my wife, I ran through Pioneer Square to King Street Station.

At King Street Station, I boarded the 5:45pm S Line train bound for Lakewood. Unlike Link trains that afternoon , the Sounder train stayed on schedule and we pulled into Tacoma around 6:40pm. I crossed the street to board the T Line, the final Sound Transit service of the day. This left just two more transit modes: Pierce Transit local bus service and the Stream Community Line. Both local buses and the Stream Community Line serve the Pacific Ave corridor, so I exited the T Line train at Convention Center station and walked over to Pacific Ave & S 14th St. A Route 1 bus showed up first so I hopped aboard and rode it two stops to Pacific & 19th. After a few other buses came and went, the last southbound Stream Community Line bus for the day stopped at Pacific & 19th.

I boarded the final bus of the speedrun and took it one stop to Tacoma Dome station. After alighting the bus I stopped the timer to record the first ever ORCA speedrun time: 9 hours, 12 minutes, and 40 seconds.

I really enjoyed spending the day exploring cities across Puget Sound and observing how different transit services are used. The passengers and drivers I spoke with were extremely kind and helpful. I was most surprised by the Kitsap Transit ferries. Every ferry trip I observed was on-time and busy (except for the return trip from Annapolis). Given the geography, the ferries offer a shortcut across the water. These smaller (and cheaper) vessels can provide better service than WSF at a fraction of the cost. More cities and counties should be allowed to operate a fleet of passenger-only ferries. The 35% service reduction in the Seattle – Bremerton Fast Ferry route is incredibly disappointing.

Another highlight of the trip was seeing how an agency’s various transit services benefit the various types of trips. No transit mode is one-size-fits-all so agencies need to adapt the vehicle types (train, bus, boat) to fit their needs. One example of this was in Lynnwood, where Route 166 and the Orange Line cover the same route between Hwy 99 and Lynnwood Transit Center. Despite sharing the same road, the Orange Line only has one stop while Route 166 has four. The Route 166 bus I was on let passengers on/off at three of the four stops. These passengers would have been overlooked with only Orange Line service and Orange Line trips would be much slower with many more stops. The overlapping local and Swift service complement each other nicely. Pierce Transit uses a similar strategy on Pacific Ave with Route 1 and the Stream Community Line.
Here is the complete list of transit services included in the ORCA speedrun:

While most transit agencies in the ORCA pod offer more flexible transit options, the ORCA speedrun only includes fixed route transit. This is primarily to minimize the impact on other transit riders. Flexible services, such as Metro Flex, CT’s Zip Shuttle, or PT’s Runner service, have limited resources. Someone using those services for a speedrun could cause a longer wait for someone else. Fixed route options are acceptable because the impact of one extra rider is negligible.

While planning this adventure I went back and forth on including King County Metro shuttle routes. Metro operates four shuttle routes, but only one (Valley Shuttle) operates year-round. The other three (Waterfront, Golden Gardens, and the snow shuttle) are seasonal or weather dependent. To add another wrinkle, this is an ORCA speedrun and the Waterfront Shuttle is completely free. Ultimately, I decided to make shuttle routes optional.

Also, I chose to separate the T Line from the 1 Line and 2 Line. While they are all technically part of Link, the T Line has little in common with the 1 Line and 2 Line. Another reason to separate the Link lines: Sound Transit reports T Line ridership data to the FTA separate from the 1 Line and 2 Line.
If you plan on attempting this challenge, I hope you can beat my time. Here are a few other rules I followed:

I hope my successful speedrun inspires other Seattle transit enthusiasts to try it as well. While Link receives more of our collective attention than any other mode, trains, buses, and boats throughout Puget Sound play a critical role in getting people where they need to go. Riding each mode is a great way to understand the value it provides to its passengers and to the overall network.

articles.title: Fare gates coming to Capitol Hill Station in $87M Sound Transit pilot
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: LA Metro installed new fare gates last year
Fare gates will greet riders at Capitol Hill Station by 2029 or 2030, following a vote by the Sound Transit board.
The changes will be part of an $87 million pilot program to install fare gates across 14 stations on the 1 Line and 2 Line .

The vote marks a major philosophical shift for Sound Transit where officials held for years that the cost of installing and maintaining a fare gate system would exceed revenue. Currently, Sound Transit operates under an open proof-of-payment structure across its 60-mile, 50-station network, maintaining a systemwide farebox recovery of around 11% to 14% — about half its goal.
Now, Sound Transit says, expansion, massively high rates of fare evasion, and some new math add up to a new equation.

“A new implementation study (PDF) published earlier this year determined that fare gates make financial sense now that the Link system has expanded,” the Sound Transit announcement reads. “Specifically, estimates show a breakeven point for capital and operational expenses at around two to three years after fare gate implementation.”
Sound Transit says gates have the potential “to significantly increase fare compliance rates and fare revenues.”
The change also comes amid continued public safety concerns around the system’s trains and open-access platforms.
The stations planned to be part of the fare gate pilot

Capitol Hill is one of nine core tunnel and high-traffic stations selected for the pilot, alongside International District/Chinatown, Pioneer Square, Symphony, Westlake, University of Washington, U District, Roosevelt, and Northgate. Five additional stations –SeaTac/Airport, Bellevue Downtown, Lynnwood City Center, Downtown Redmond, and Federal Way Downtown — will also receive gates.

Despite what your libertarian neighbor might think, no major urban transit system has 100% farebox recovery as a goal. A 22% farebox recovery goal means Sound Transit only expects fare revenue to cover 22 cents of every dollar spent on day-to-day light rail operations — the remaining 78% is subsidized by local taxes.
The fare gates pilot could provide the agency a path to finally meeting its mark.

The approval of the pilot comes in a whirlwind year of changed plans for Sound Transit. Earlier this year, the board approved a major package of deferrals and cuts t o address a projected $34.5 billion shortfall. The new financial outlook would have Sound Transit on track for expansion to West Seattle by 2032 and Ballard by 2042.

Meanwhile, light rail has now reached the Central District as Judkins Park Station celebrated its grand opening in March, part of a full transformation into a two-line system — the original 1 Line serving the city and its north-south neighbors, and now the added 2 Line connecting Seattle to Bellevue and Redmond on the world’s first light rail on a floating bridge.
The system has seen a major jump in ridership with the expansion including Capitol Hill Station where boardings have settled around 11,000 per day — about 40% above pre-pandemic levels.
Sound Transit fare ambassadors added platform checks in 2024 but non-payment remains an issue (Image: Sound Transit)
Sound Transit is giving itself a few years to sort out the mechanics and finances of the new fare plan including what kind of gates will be installed.

Some things are known. Under the planned system, Capitol Hill riders must tap ORCA cards and phones at designated entry and exit gates. Other elements including what manufacturer will pick up the contract are still to come.

Sound Transit estimates the $87 million program will reach a financial break-even point within two to three years after deployment. Its models project that the gates will generate between $33 million and $83 million in additional fare revenue per year.
Sound Transit uses a flat-fare system for the Link 1 Line and 2 Line with $3.00 one-way fare for adults, age 19 to 64. Income-qualified riders and seniors board for $1.

Sound Transit is starting with 14 sub-surface stations because street-level platforms can create dangerous track-crossing hazards if fenced off, while enclosed hubs like Capitol Hill are far easier and safer to retrofit. Focusing on these initial high-ridership stops captures roughly 85% of riders for $87 million, allowing the agency to test fare technology, accessibility, and financial returns before committing to a more costly systemwide buildout.
The rollout will also adjust on-site personnel duties. Sound Transit projects Fare Ambassadors will reduce enforcement hours by 44% and increase passenger assistance time by 33%.

articles.title: Capitol Hill’s summer politics were quiet — The fall ballot fights will not be
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Pedersen’s easy August win. You can explore the Primary Election Results maps here thanks to the Washington Community Alliance.
While area leaders all but have their campaign races tied up headed into November there will still be a busy fall political season across Capitol Hill and the Central District.

Maps from the August primary tell the story of the highest profile individual seat up for grabs on Capitol Hill. Two-decade incumbent State Sen. Jamie Pedersen’s 67% showing in the primary is evident in the results for each election precinct across Capitol Hill and most of his 43rd District save for the blocks of central Broadway where first-time challenger and “Tax the Rich” proponent Hannah Sabio-Howell managed a flat-footed tie.

CHS reported here on the funding surge behind Pedersen, the party’s current Majority Leader in the state Senate, an architect of the Millionaires Tax , and a veteran lawmaker who has been part of 43rd District leadership for twenty years, as state Democratic leaders helped lock down the race. Institutional donors and statewide PACs can now shift their war chests to competitive general election battlegrounds elsewhere in the state.

Despite the distant second place finish, Sabio-Howell still has a race to run, nipping at Pedersen’s flank. “Our opponent & the establishment that backs him spent $500,000 to try to drown us out. So what do we do from now to November 3rd? Get louder. Demand better from a state controlled entirely by Democrats,” she said in a campaign update. “Reject false choices between funding one priority at the expense of another. Refuse to accept bold action that only precedes an election year.”
“The pundits are giving their takes about races like ours, so here’s a take from us,” read another. “Nothing moves if we don’t push, and no one spends $500k if they’re not scared of us.”
While spending on the 43rd District race will undoubtedly cool. the major push to strengthen turnout and support here for statewide political battles on the fall ballot is just getting started.

Initiative 001 seeks to restore parental rights measures regarding public school curriculum review, record access, and parental notifications for student health services while Initiative 638 proposes prohibiting transgender girls from participating in girls’ school sports and instituting biological sex verification requirements for student athletes.
King County turnout in the August Primary dropped from 2022’s poor showing

Both measures bring debates over schools, parental notification, and transgender youth participation in sports from state legislatures to statewide ballot initiatives and both will seek overwhelming opposition and turnout in strongholds like Capitol Hill and Seattle.
CHS reported earlier this year on the Capitol Hill-based Gender Justice League’s work to help lead the state’s pushback against the initiatives.
Campaigns will also see Capitol Hill’s younger, more likely to rent voters as a potential center of strength in a key Seattle ballot battle.
The 2026 Seattle Transit Measure proposes a 10-year renewal funded by a 0.3% sales tax championed by Mayor Katie Wilson to allow the city to purchase increased bus service on key routes.

If approved by voters, officials say the proposal will expand Seattle’s capacity from 180,000 to 280,000 annual bus trips — a 47% increase in total service. The plan boosts frequencies on 10 to 15 key routes, expands late-night and weekend service, and prioritizes electric buses in South Seattle and the Duwamish Valley. The measure will “double the number of free ORCA cards provided to low-income households” by expanding subsidized passes to 12,000 additional residents, while allocating funds to “support the recommendations of the King County Regional Transit Safety Task Force.”

The proposed sales tax bump arrives amid grumbles of tax fatigue in the region. For a median two-person Seattle household, approval would mean a jump from about $29 to around $58 a year at the register.

If approved, Seattle’s total combined sales tax rate would reach 10.80% — 6.5% to the general state fund, 3.9% to city public safety, housing, and cultural services, the newly approved 0.10% sales tax starting in 2027 to fund county road repair and maintenance, and 0.30% to the renewed levy.

Campaigns looking for any Capitol Hill and Central District boosts will hope these issues will motivate voters to get involved. Across King County as a whole, turnout in the August Primary was a dismal 37%.
The General Election is Tuesday, November 3rd.

articles.title: The Best Things To Do in Seattle This Month: September 2026
articles.author: EverOut Staff
paras: School is starting, apples are ripening, and the days are getting ever-so-slightly shorter, but it’s technically still summer until September 22. That means you have almost the whole month to soak up those precious last golden hours of the season at outdoor festivals, ease into fall with exciting performances and book releases, and simply enjoy Seattle’s endless array of happenings. As we do every month, we’ve compiled the biggest events you need to know about in every genre, from The Kehlani World Tour to Weezer and from the 29th Annual Local Sightings Film Festival to The Stranger’s 2026 Genius Awards .

Hannibal Buress My affinity for Hannibal Buress stems back to the Eric Andre Show , where he gifted the world with ridiculous quotes like “Morpheus drinking a 40 in a death basket” and, one of my favorites, “Y’all spin around like ballers, seething with jealousy I am.” But Buress is just as funny (if not more so) on stage. Throughout his storied career, the Chicago native has released side-splitting specials like Animal Furnace , Comedy Camisado , and Miami Nights , written for SNL and 30 Rock , and popped up in cameos all over the place, from Broad City to Spider-Man: Homecoming . Even outside the comedy circuit, he’s just as prolific in music, releasing ridiculous (and surprisingly catchy) tunes under the rap moniker Eshu Tune . If you’re into weird, dry, unpredictable humor, his stand-up show is a must-see. LANGSTON THOMAS Neptune Theatre, University District (Fri Sept 4)

articles.title: The New Seattle Transit Measure Could Make Night Buses Function
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Chris Moore, the production manager at Chop Suey in Capitol Hill, has a hell of a time getting home on public transit after his shift.

In Seattle, a city doing the least to fight its early-to-bed reputation, the last light rail train stops running at approximately 1 a.m. and service does not resume before 4 a.m. A handful of buses operate between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. buses, but most run only once every hour, with a few twice-an-hour exceptions. It makes getting home from a concert, a bender, or a graveyard shift a grade-school word problem.

On weekdays, Moore finishes work—booking, bartending, doing sound, and balancing the books—after midnight. On Saturdays, once the last ravers have retired and he wraps everything up, he’s not homeward bound until 4:30 a.m. Pretty much all of his coworkers drive to work and brave the nightmare (financial, logistical) of parking on Capitol Hill. Moore does, too. Except on Thursdays when his partner has dibs on their shared car. If he’s lucky, and manages to catch the last light rail train and his bus to Fremont arrives on time, or at all, the journey will take an hour.. Usually, it’s a longer ordeal; if the buses don’t show, he ends up forking over $40 for an Uber anyway.
“I don’t know why it’s so inconsistent for someone that works a nighttime job to rely on public transit,” Moore says. “It’s great during the day.”

That much is not a mystery: Transit systems focus on funding frequent bus service during peak-service hours when people are commuting to and from work or school. The lack of investment in nighttime transit strands workers and revelers alike, forcing people to drive, overspend on a Lyft, hurting the city’s nighttime economy in the process.

And yet, nighttime service in the area is better than it’s ever been. Last week, King County Metro added a few new nighttime routes in its fall service changes and the South Link Connections project to its Night Owl bus system. Sound Transit also added two new night buses that run every 30 minutes along the light rail lines while trains are not in service.

But that’s still not enough for Moore to ditch his car permanently, or for his coworkers who live in Kent to bus to and from work. Moore wishes the light rail would at least run late on weekends, but Sound Transit says it needs those late night hours for maintenance. Buses can fill the gaps, but the frequency and reliability isn’t there yet. Even though parking costs and car payments are expensive, commuting by car is a sure thing at the end of a late night.
One thing transit advocates and legislators think could help is the new version of the Seattle Transit Measure (STM).

Voters last approved this sales tax to fund bus service, transit access programs, and capital projects in Seattle in 2020. In July, the Seattle City Council approved the biggest STM in the tax’s 12-year existence, doubling the tax and extending its typical lifespan by four years. If Seattle voters approve the 0.3 percent sales tax this November, the city will double the amount it spends on Metro bus service—from $50 million to $100 million—amounting to 100,000 additional bus service hours over the next 10 years.

When the Seattle City Council discussed the proposed STM , Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck included an amendment that stressed the importance of steering funds toward increasing overnight bus service. The council can’t actually direct the funds, but they can set it as a priority that the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) can implement, Rinck says, speaking in a personal capacity. The amendment is more vibes than strict policy. There is no specific allocation amount for nighttime bus service outlined in the amendment, but Rinck is hopeful it’ll result in more nighttime service hours.

“Fingers crossed that voters say yes, and then in the next year we’ll see which buses will go from having 10-minute wait times to seven-minute or five-minute wait times, and which buses get expanded into late-night service as well,” Rinck says.

Her hopes are based in precedent. The STM is responsible for the existing King County Metro nighttime service. With a bigger pot of STM funds to pull from, those services should expand. Since its inception, the STM has helped make buses people rely on available at non-peak hours according to Kirk Hovenkotter, the executive director of Transportation Choices Coalition.

In the early 2010s, the night routes were “these really circuitous, silly, routes” that weren’t direct or quick, he says. The first STM in 2014 caused a “big shift” with investments in late-night service on routes such as the Rapid Ride H line, which runs from Seattle to Burien, or the 7, which runs from downtown to Rainier Beach, and the 49, which goes from the University District to Downtown through Capitol Hill.
“Night buses actually were seen as not this measure of last resort,” Hovenkotter says.

The current STM funds 63 percent of Metro’s 19 existing Night Owl routes , according to King County Metro spokesperson Al Sanders. Those routes include the 44, the 48, and the 70, to name a few, plus every late night Rapid Ride route except the A. (Six of Metro’s eight Rapid Ride routes have late-night service.)
The big STM on November’s ballot should add even more bus service to nighttime and weekend bus routes, especially since those hours are actually the cheapest to buy for Seattle, Hovenkotter says.

“It’s really expensive to buy more service during those [peak hours] because every Metro bus is already out there,” Hovenkotter says. “But there’s a bunch of buses that are just sitting, waiting to be used on weekends or late nights. So the city is being really smart at using these STM dollars to buy those hours.”

For people like Anna Zivarts, the founder of Nondrivers Alliance, who, shockingly, doesn’t drive at all, having reliable nighttime transportation is truly an accessibility issue. “I want to be able to get home whenever I want and not feel trapped,” she says.

Rinck is familiar with that trapped feeling. Not long ago, Rinck worked at a restaurant in Lower Queen Anne Uptown near Key Arena Climate Pledge Arena. Similar to Moore at Chop Suey, Rinck would get off work and have to wait in the dark and cold for upwards of an hour for a bus to take her home.
“All you want to do after working a long shift is be home,” Rinck says.

Perhaps, the STM can help make that happen, and in doing so, make Seattle a city that can stay up past its bedtime, and help help the nighttime economy, says Scott Plusquellec, Seattle’s Nightlife Business Advocate, also known by his unofficial title (which he does not like, but I do), the Night Mayor.

“It would transform the city if we had more late night transit,” Plusquellec, the Night Mayor (sorry, Scott), says. His “great white whale” is getting the light rail to run longer. That’s not happening any time soon, or at all, so, it’s up to the buses.

“It would go a long way towards making us a 24-hour city,” Plusquellec says. “When the buses stop running and people can’t get around, then they’re either just going to stay in their own neighborhoods close to their home, or they’re not going out.”
Why buy a concert ticket, or a movie ticket, or meet friends at a bar, when getting home is a puzzle they have to solve tired and drunk? People choose to stay in, he says.

“That’s a ticket that’s not bought. That’s drinks that aren’t bought. That’s the dinner that wasn’t bought,” Plusquellec says. “You are deflating people’s ability to go out because they don’t have the option.”

Workers are the other side of the equation. Seattle doesn’t have a full picture of how many people work nighttime jobs. Plusquellec’s department in the Seattle Office of Economic Development will soon publish a study on overnight workers. He hopes the data can inform future nighttime transit route improvements.

articles.title: On Pike and Nowhere
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: The most 86ed man in Seattle . The friends of Tom Barnes agree about that. They rattle off an incomplete list: He was definitely banned from Big Mario’s once, as well as the old Comet, where he tumbled off the bar and broke a leg. He was barred from Saint John’s for years at a time, once because he’d crashed through the glass in the front door, the other times because he’d left the water running in his apartment upstairs, causing the establishment to flood—on three separate occasions. At some point, he realized the entire Saint John’s staff had turned over; with no one left to remember the debacle, he was free to patronize the joint again.

A few weeks ago, a small group of friends gathered on the back patio of Saint John’s Bar and Eatery. Surrounded by an army of plastic dinosaurs crouched in the grass, they discussed plans for his memorial, and to reminisce. The 74-year-old artist had passed away, unexpectedly, in early July.

Seated to my right was his neighbor and fellow artist who lived across the hall, Katlyn Hubner ; Diana Adams, owner of Vermillion Art Gallery and Bar ; Rob Joynes, a poet, musician, bartender, and Barnes’ accidental best friend (and the recipient of bottomless late-night texts); and Steve Gilbert , who met Barnes in the ’90s and exhibited his work multiple times at his eponymous gallery . Later came two who knew Barnes in the ’70s, when he first arrived to the Pacific Northwest from Toledo, Ohio and became enmeshed in the local theater scene. Even his landlord came to pay his respects.

I knew Barnes, but not like they did. Memories spilled out. The group blinked back tears and broke into chuckles over absurd anecdotes. There was also a profound sense of helplessness and frustration at the randomness of his death. I could sympathize: This will be the second memorial I’ve attended in two months that was the result of an accidental fentanyl overdose. Groping for a way to process grief or place blame feels impossible.
“He was loved and hated by many,” says Adams. She herself had kicked Barnes out of Vermillion more than once—a “soft 86”—when he’d gotten too rowdy.

“It took me a while to really get him,” Hubner says. “Barnes’s delivery was sarcastic, blunt. He’s a crass son of a bitch. But he took me in when I was homeless, he was always there for me. He was also my biggest cheerleader, always pushing me to hit that damn studio. He was always pumping you up, like, Keep going, kids, just stop fucking people, just keep painting! ”

Barnes was an artist’s artist: a documentarian, bohemian, romantic, poet. He was estranged from his blood family; we aren’t sure why, but even his chosen family drew boundaries. One of his friends has penned an “O-Bitch-uary” to be read at the memorial. Barnes lived to party. He also lived in pain. He died from complications of both. When Barnes was found in his apartment a few days after his death, the police locked the door and took the keys. They explained that, with no known next of kin and without a will, his possessions would pass to the state.
His friends panicked. The life’s work of a man for whom they cared deeply, despite his foibles, lay on the other side of the door. They were the only ones standing between archive and obliteration.

Joynes spent the next three days glued to his computer, scouring public records, going down social media rabbit holes, and calling every person that might provide a clue about blood relatives, dead or alive. He gradually mapped a network of friends and acquaintances that spanned decades. Someone recalled Barnes mentioning a sister at one point. But Barnes is a helluva common name. Joynes kept at it, and the sleuthing paid off: Barnes had a sister all along, estranged and living in Kirkland for the past 40 years. With her blessing, they were given keys to his apartment and possessions.

The group left Saint John’s Bar and walked around the corner to the entrance of Saint John’s Apartments. We entered and filed into a tiny studio on the ground floor. Barnes did not live here, but his work did, temporarily, with the landlord’s approval. It was overwhelming, seeing it all like that. Over 800 artworks—most on paper: drawings, paintings, and collages contained in sketchbooks and archival portfolios. It also felt strikingly small—a life compressed like this.
When describing Barnes’ work, nothing is more apropos than “fever dream.”

Characters and scenes from real life are rendered in a kind of naive, psychedelic, art-brut mannerism with the tweaky energy of a 6-year-old. But allow your eyes to adjust, and the impeccability of the composition becomes evident; there’s not a blobby figure, rogue blot, or dot without purpose. Scratchy outlines made with a Uniball pen are the scaffolding of each image, which is fleshed out in obscenely bright colors—acrid yellows, blood-letting scarlet, and neon green—with a childlike flatness. Other times, a murky haze of chalk-white overpaint lends an atmospheric depth. Amid the wet-on-wet chaos of colors, the image is abruptly punctuated by the most intricate details of bottles lined up in a fridge beyond the bar or the pattern on a frock. Occasionally, stickers and other sparkly things find their way into the picture frame. Barnes’s style is the definition of febrile. If once there was a hinge, it had come off, or was hanging by a thread.

You can tell he channeled the ghost of Ralph Steadman at some point, but had passed through and arrived on the other side, into uncharted territory and a cosmology populated by artists, dancers, friends, tavern regulars, and hot girls. He loved women, a passion as complex as everything else about him.

“One thing I think is misunderstood about his aesthetic and his artistic vision is that he was obsessed with muses and the scandalousness of youth,” says Joynes. “But I don’t think it was as perverse as people might think. I think he was always trying to capture the human experience, and human experience can be ugly, it can be bad. I think he loved the grotesque.”

Barnes only drew from human experience, never from photos. He called his documentary body of work Drawing on the Run. Some series chronicled his travels across Mexico, Cambodia, and New Orleans, but many are scenes from Capitol Hill. Series like Seattle Celebrities , Vermillion , and Pike and Nowhere are full of familiar faces: Lelah Maupin, Bethany Jean Clement, Timothy Rysdyke, Mimi Allen, Siolo Thompson, Kelly O, Casey Weldon, Ezra Dickinson. Liz Orth, Lisa Prank, and Zoe Scofield. And places: Chop Suey, the Royal Room, Vito’s, Bait Shop, Bimbo’s, Cha Cha, Cafe Racer, Vermillion, The Annex Theatre, Noc Noc, Comet Tavern, Pony, the Frye Art Museum.

Older work veered into collage. Entire volumes were dedicated to antifascist meditations, like his collection of anti-Iraq war collages, WATCHING THE WAR DRUNK. I was shocked to come across drawings rendered in an academic style; not only could he do the unhinged stuff, he could properly chiaroscuro the hell out of a figure. Barnes held a BFA in performing arts, theater, and painting from Evergreen State College. He lived and worked in New York City in the ’70s. He attended Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on a scholarship. The naive quality of his work emerged intentionally, over time.

“What he and I had in common was that he was one of those burning people who just could not stop creating obsessively,” Joynes says. “Art was just inside of him. And when I started to put together what his influences were—he started lending me books by Frank O’Hara, Henry Miller—that’s when I realized he’s like old-school Hemingway, like a dog. He’s like an old-dog artist. They don’t make ’em like that anymore—the last of his kind.”

Of course, there’s an argument to be made that the old-school Hemingways are best left in the dustbin of the last century. Yet, there is something about Barnes’s dogged, all-consuming dedication to art that is enviable.

At one point in 2020, Barnes told me that he’d made a portrait of myself and my eventual husband. He’d caught us, 8-by-8-inch sketchbook in hand, during a drizzly Juneuary at a Pride concert on the Hill. I was dumbfounded by the result. He depicted me in a striped shirt I definitely was not wearing. Likewise, my “bestie” (as per the painting’s title) is wearing a pirate hat with skull and crossbones and a neon green shirt he was also definitely not wearing. My eye sockets are black scribbles. An impossibly giant pink butterfly (also not there) hovers over my head. According to his site, it was sold at some point, I have no idea to whom. When I look at the image now, I can see what he perceived: two besotted bohemian pirates enjoying a rainy Seattle summer. Too much black eyeliner. It looked exactly like us.

I find myself returning to a passage from Chris Kraus’s 1999 essay “Pussy Orphanage”: “When an artist dies before his or her time, who manages the estate and how, becomes vitally important.” She continues: “Altruism aside, how is it that any artist’s work will come to survive for others in the future? Works of art, after all, are mute and can’t speak for themselves.”

Barnes’s chosen family—the poets, artists, bar owners, and hell-raisers—are speaking for the art. A retrospective of rescued work will be on view at Vermillion, a place he loved, through October 3. It is aptly titled The road goes on forever and the party never ends . The man chose his family well.
The road goes on forever and the party never ends is on view at Vermillion Art Gallery and Bar through October 3. A memorial will be held September 5.

articles.title: Slog AM: A Private Detective is Hunting a Killer, the Bounty Hunters are Hunting in the Streets, and We’re Back to Hunting the Hun
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: Museum of History and Industry workers are unionizing: Workers at Seattle’s premier local history museum announced yesterday they intend to join the Communication Workers of America, citing “opacity in decision making and ineffective leadership from executive management, lack of benefits for part time and on-call workers, chronic understaffing, unsustainable workloads, minimal professional development or training, and wage stagnation despite rising living costs and unmet promises of improvement.”

In addition, “Workers report that trust in senior leadership, as well as staff morale, has steadily declined as major hiring decisions and organizational changes have been made with little to no staff input. They further allege that workers who have raised concerns around ethics, staff capacity, and institutional sustainability, have experienced retaliation.”

Employees walk out at Washington’s largest employer (which is Washington): As promised, Washington’s unionized state workers walked out en masse yesterday in protest of the state refusing to raise wages during recent rounds of contract negotiations. Governor Bob Ferguson pledged not to raise taxes and instead cut costs heading into an economic slump to cover the rising cost of state services. This is austerity spiraling 101, but there’s someone he forgot to ask.

Seattle teachers strike tomorrow if no deal reached today: A similar story is playing out in Seattle schools, which are supposed to open for the new academic year tomorrow if only the school district would answer the demands of local teachers. We’re entering the mud-slinging phase as both sides try to convince struggling parents that it’s the other’s fault. Spoiler alert: It’s the school district’s fault, not the teachers’. Yell at the government.

The streets are extended gutters and the gutters are full of blood and when the drains finally scab over, all the vermin will drown: There’s been a goose murder. The case is a mess. Conspiracy theories are flying like feathers. Right near MOHAI, when they’re organizing? A suspect in a Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace “No Nerds, No Birds” shirt during the union’s contract negotiations with Boeing? And the victim is a Canada goose, in this geopolitical climate? This ain’t no matrimonial snoop job. The Stranger’s own Nathalie Graham has the story of the private detective on the case, Naia Okami.
“I’m not your typical gruff ex-cop. I’m early 30s. I dress emo. I listen to emo music. I’m in alt-communities. I don’t look like I do this sort of work, but I do,” she says.

“Chaotic ambush by bounty hunters” is not the kind of thing you want to read about your neighborhood: Nor do you want to hear bounty hunters yell “Tase him again, Tase him again!” as an RV careens toward your property. North Seattle residents were not so lucky last week. Seattle police appear mostly concerned with explaining how none of this is their fault, per the Seattle Times . As a quick reminder, bounty hunting is not something that other countries do. It is crazy American gun culture nonsense, which is why the only other country where it’s legal is our long-suffering Philippine colony.

Candidate for Senate walks back lie that he “saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes: Former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers did not in fact see the body with his own eyes. As the chair of the House intelligence committee at the time of bin Laden’s assassination by the United States, he instead saw a photograph. The Guardian reports “Rogers said—days after the raid—that the photograph he’d seen made it clear that Bin Laden was dead. But he said he supported Obama’s decision to not make the graphic images of the raid public.”

The photos were too graphic to release because, according to The Intercept , Navy SEAL Rob O’Neill (whose DUI charge I covered as a cub reporter in his hometown of Butte, MT) ritualistically mutilated bin-Laden’s corpse in grotesque SEAL tradition by blasting his brains out all over his face.

Interbay has a lead problem: Not as bad as Butte’s, where a copper smelter that electrified America dumped it onto everyone’s kids for years, but bad enough there’s signs all along a street near Fisherman’s Terminal warning about it. Lead is especially bad for kids, it messes with their developing minds. None of this is good for the kids at the daycare across from Dyno Battery. Details in the Seattle Times .

A proper deep dive on the Gravel teens now working for OpenAI: Remember that annoying viral socialist political campaign backing the ancient former US senator from Alaska Mike Gravel for president? Well, the two teenagers behind it now work in the AI industry, according to a thorough CNN look at their dumb asses. This is a good reminder: Do not trust overly-online leftist political actors disconnected from real social movements, they are not “close to the people,” as Mao once said. They cannot unite the peasantry and free China.

Trump socializes Venezuela’s oil for Americans: Speaking of failed left-wing social movements no longer close to the people, Bolivarianism is not looking so hot these days. Gustavo Petro is out in Colombia, and over the weekend the Trump administration announced a new partnership with the ruling United Socialist Party of Venezuela that basically amounts to the US Department of Defense stealing the country’s oil because Trump thinks it will make shortages from the Iran War negligible (this won’t work). This is all, of course, downstream, down the Orinoco , to the shores of Tripoli of the US kidnapping Venezuela’s democratically-elected President Nicolas Maduro. He posted a jail selfie over the weekend.
Somehow Kaiser Wilhelm has returned: This is how reactionary mainstream politics have become.

It was the 21st anniversary of Hurricane Katrina this weekend: The nicest people in America’s greatest city took the brunt of the storm, which you can get an eyewitness view of in the fantastic documentary Trouble the Water free on Kanopy with an equally free Seattle Public Library card. The hurricane coincided with the beginning of the school year, so my introduction to high school was watching footage of the devastation and thinking “wow I feel bad for whoever has to clean that up” only for it to turn out to be me a few years later. RIP to AmeriCorps NCCC’s Southern Region base in Mississippi, another victim of DOGE. You were the second-most progressive thing the federal government ever did in Vicksburg.
