articles.title: Winter Rollback of Pike Place Market Pedestrian Pilot Moves Forward
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Last week, the Pike Place Market Historical Commission gave its unanimous approval to planned adjustments around vehicle access through Seattle's iconic market. Set to be in effect from October through next March, the adjustments represent the newest phase of a pedestrian pilot program that has been in effect for nearly 18 months, but have been lambasted as a retreat on an issue that has widespread city support – restricting unnecessary car traffic through the market.

Under the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) plan , the main corridor along Pike Place will only experience "soft closures" on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, with the hours vehicles are restricted slightly tightened up to 11am to 4pm. Soft closures mean access is restricted to delivery vehicles, ADA access for disabled patrons, and market vendors.

Apart from major event days when the street will fully close with barricades, through car traffic will be unrestricted along the street with "street closed" signage switched to signage telling drivers to yield to pedestrians.

Pointing to a SDOT survey conducted earlier this year showing 98% support for maintaining vehicle barriers through the Market, a sizable contingent of Seattle urbanists have lamented the move as a backslide that isn't in alignment with the broader city's desires for a more pedestrian-oriented Pike Place. But many Market vendors have argued that they weren't included in the initial launch of the pedestrian pilot in April of 2025, a move made in response to a utility repair project along Stewart Street.

"There are a lot of strong feelings and ideas that we heard from a lot of different people. So, I think ideas are as diverse and dynamic as the number of businesses in the market and all the people who also use this street," Radcliffe Dacanay, the SDOT project manager who has been tasked with leading this work at Pike Place, told commissioners. "There were some increased sales [that] some vendors expressed, but not all vendors experienced increased sales. So, that data is varied. Some sales improved, some vendors [it did] not. But also, just this sense of the Market as a place to come to, and not just an errand space."

The historic commission does get final buy-off on changes of either use or design within the seven-acre historic district. But SDOT's recommendation for the pilot's next phase came about after months of discussions with Market power players, including the commission's chair Jon Cracolici, Alex Hudson from Mayor Katie Wilson's office, members of the Pike Place Merchant's Association (rebooted just this year after being defunct for years), and representatives for the Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA) which directly maintains operations along the street.

During the meeting, PDA Chief Operating Officer Katie Trent framed the winter access plan as an improvement over last winter, because the PDA had not been enforcing vehicle access restrictions on any weekdays through the Market's quieter months. Trent's comments gloss over the change in signage that will fairly explicitly encourage drivers to head down Pike Place
Trent also provided a new counterpoint to the positive sales data seen at the market in 2025, when it comes to year-over-year (YOY) data for the first half of 2026.

Between January and June, visits to the Market from local residents coming less than 30 miles declined by 11% compared to 2025, a trend that only started to reverse itself in July, with a 1% YOY increase seen in that month. Over those six months, total sales did continue to increase at the Market, but growth slowed from 7% in 2025 to 4.7% this year. Grocery sales took at 4.5% hit during the second quarter, a fact that can likely be traced to the shift in visitor trends during the FIFA Men's World Cup.

"There's all kinds of things that can contribute to what goes on with visitation and sales data, but the street has been an element in there," Trent said. "We have vendors coming to us and saying, 'I'm losing customers because of this, especially in the offseason. Why is the street closed?' That's impactful to what we want to promote as the operator."

The shift toward seasonal operations was bolstered by a study conducted by the University of Washington's Urban Freight Lab – a study that makes some leaps on the way to getting to its conclusions, based on the fact that fewer people visit the Market in the winter overall than in the summer. But it became clear during Wednesday's meeting that SDOT and the PDA had come together to land on a threshold of Market visitation to justify the new schedule: 3,300 Market visitors per hour, or around 55 people passing through the street every minute.
During the summer months, that threshold has been easily met, but in the slower months it has not, according to PDA data from 2025.

Despite presenting the methodology behind the proposal, some merchants and commenters – including members of the advocacy nonprofit group Friends of the Market – wanted to drop soft closures on Fridays. That point of contention pushed this proposal toward looking more like a compromise. It's important to note that the PDA is also empowered to restrict vehicle access if foot traffic is more than expected – and in turn, to cancel soft closures early if the Market is a ghost town on a Friday in February.

"I support this plan. I thought it was very thoughtfully put together. As a vendor, I felt included in the process, both by Urban Freight Lab and the PDA and the working group. I really appreciate what SDOT did in hearing our needs and continues to," Bite Society owner Lendy Hensley said. "I didn't get everything I wanted in this. I suspect no one did, and sometimes I think that is the best kind of agreement. I hope the process continues, as somebody who's looking at Fridays and thinking maybe not that. So I'm hoping for continued conversation as we get to see what these winter months actually look like with this framework in mind."
Plenty of speakers at last week's meeting did provide a voice for the idea of keeping the pedestrian pilot in effect seven days a week.

"I think the thing that I was very disappointed in when I moved to the Market is how uncomfortable it was to shop at the Market and to walk down the streets and try to find my way through the sidewalks," resident Larry Goetz said. "I really appreciate what SDOT did in closing the traffic for the last year and a half, I think it has worked beautifully, especially for the World Cup games. I think it really works. I would like to see it continue."

What happens this winter will likely only set the stage for the Market's next new normal, with SDOT set to return to the commission in January for a proposal for what next summer looks like at Pike Place, without a World Cup to plan around. But at some point, the pilot will need to draw to a close, shifting to a more permanent program.

"I hope that we don't do this every six months," commissioner Mark Childs said ahead of Wednesday's vote. "That this actually builds to something that can last for a period of time, and that there's certainty that people can build around."

articles.title: Link Ends Earlier, Starts Later
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: Several comments have raised concerns that the August 29th service change shortened Link’s service day, so that it now ends earlier and starts later. This interacts with the launch of ST Express “Night Ride” routes between midnight and 4am. These theoretically can replace Link trips. But the ST Express routes bypass several high-ridership Seattle Link stations. This can force trips that were on Link in the midnight hour or 11 pm hour or 4 am hour to an ST Express or Metro route, turn a 1-seat ride into a 2-seat ride, and the bus routes are less frequent than Link was.

I wanted to know, did the spans really change on August 29? What is the current situation on weekdays, Saturdays, and Sundays? What kinds of trips at what hours are newly 2-seat rides? Where is the best place to live to have the earliest or latest Link service? Which can you go to on those lucky runs?

I looked at the new 1 Line and 2 Line schedules to quantify the current situation and changes. To reach these pages from Sound Transit’s website, use the schedule form on the home page to get to the interactive charts. To get a PDF of the schedule, go to the bottom of the page and press the “Full Schedule PDF” button.
I tried to make a consolidated list that would organize the first/last runs in different areas and days. But it was an insanely difficult job, and after a few hours I gave up.
So instead we’re going to crowdsource the issue.

How has Link’s span changed since August 29th? Has this affected your trips? Or do you see other people’s trips that are affected? Can you glean more from the schedules than I can? Can you figure out the right questions to ask AI to figure it out? (If you do, please disclose AI’s role in the result.)

Some of these impacts have already come up in recent articles’ comments, but this article is a place to consolidate them all together so we can see the total impact. And it will be a reference in the future when people have a question, so that they can find it all in one easy-to-find place.

The problem I had with the interactive schedule pages was I had to keep scrolling four directions to get at the first or last full run and short run, and when that would get you to Westlake or SeaTac or the final terminus. I had to keep going up to the date switcher. I kept finding mistake after mistake in my results, so I had to go back and reconfirm them, or compare weekday to Saturday again, and make sure I hadn’t jumped back to a date before the service change. Reading the PDFs online was a lot of up-and-down scrolling with similar printing. Printing the PDFs to get a wider-area view at once would take 34 pages per line. Maybe ST has a printed schedule book with them but I’d have to go search for a copy. I didn’t want to publish a list with mistakes that would waste everybody’s time.
Maybe if different people address small parts of the issue individually, we can get those facts more accurately and a better idea of the whole.

ST in the future wants to shorten Link’s span further, or have more single-track reductions, or more weekend closures of segments, to increase the time available for maintenance. We desperately want ST to increase maintenance because Link’s reliability is far below peer cities’ networks. This causes passengers to get stuck en route, be late for appointments, or drive to critical appointments to avoid the risk that Link will hiccup that day. It also snares visitors and gives them a negative impression of Seattle and Seattle’s transit. So we really want maintenance to be increased to make Link more reliable.

At the same time we need Link’s late-night and early-morning service. If ST Express night owls bypass several Seattle stations in the shoulder hours Link used to provide, then it’s not an adequate substitute. ST says Metro has night owl buses in all those areas (7, 36, 49, 67, 70). But those night runs are funded by Seattle’s transit levy, and will go away if voters don’t renew the levy this November. Metro stopped funding Seattle night owls in the 2014 recession. Also, the bus routes are half-hourly or hourly, as opposed to Link’s 15 minutes. If you switch to say the 49+597 or 36+597 to workaround the loss of Link, you may be waiting 30+30 minutes or a full hour.

This affects people coming home from bars, staff working at bars, people who start or end a night shift, people going to the airport for an early-morning flight, and people coming from an evening flight that was delayed and didn’t land until midnight or later, and airport workers with early-morning shifts.

So what are the actual problems now? Did Link’s span decrease August 29th? What kinds of trips, where, and when are affected? If in the future ST ends Link even earlier at 10pm or 9 pm every day or on monthly maintenance days or two-week maintenance periods, how big a deal would that be? How would we cope with it? What should we tell Sound Transit and our politicians about all this?

articles.title: Sound Transit Board Greenlights Targeted Fare Gate Retrofits
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Thursday, the Sound Transit Board of Directors approved the creation of a fare gate retrofit program set to use $6 million that has been queued up to design a gate pilot at 14 high-ridership Link stations . Those design and planning funds are expected to ultimately turn into an $87 million program that will get gates installed by 2029 or 2030.
Once implemented, the pilot program is expected to recoup costs through higher fare compliance rates within two to three years, according to agency projections.

At last estimate, Sound Transit puts its current light rail fare compliance rate at 63%, based on automatic counters on trains compared to fares paid. The caveat: that figure includes youth under 19, who are not required to pay fares under the state's free youth fare program. Adjusting for free-ride youth would put the compliance rate closer to 70%.

Additionally, Sound Transit's fare ambassador program, which is based on staff members actually checking fares on trains, has measured the fare compliance rate at 85% in 2025, with a further 7.5% of fare-less riders checked being exempt youth. This discrepancy has led some transit advocates to argue the agency is overestimating fare evasion and the potential uptick in fare revenue that gates could prompt.

Sound Transit's financial modeling is based on achieving 95% fare compliance at stations where gates are installed, which staff noted is less that the 98% peer agencies have reported at gated stations. The need to include accessible entry points for people in wheelchairs or with strollers or bikes means the opportunity for fare gate jumping will exist to some extent, although other U.S. transit agencies have estimated that problem as a relatively minor one.

Sound Transit's initial proposal would put bi-directional fare gates at the high-ridership stations in the core of Seattle, Bellevue downtown, and at the ends of lines. Since the gates would be bidirectional and require riders to tap on to enter and tap off to exit stations, staff expect compliance rates to increase systemwide, not just at the gated stations. This is because so many trips end at the stations set to receive gates. With bi-directional gates at key stations, retrofitting all of the system's other stations down the line will likely prove much less lucrative.

"It's important to highlight that while we are showing only boardings at gated and non-gated stations, we're going to need to measure system-wide compliance given the bidirectional nature of the gates, where compliance will be driven both by boardings and alightings," said Brian de Place, Sound Transit's Security and Fare Engagement Executive Director. "And since the vast majority of our riders come in and out of the gated stations, we expect to see compliance levels change at the non-gated stations as well as the gated ones."

About 85% of Sound Transit light rail ridership starts or ends at one of the 14 gates to be targeted for gates, officials said. That traffic has grown rapidly with the extension of the 2 Line across the lake, reaching 160,000 daily riders even before the World Cup came to town.

De Place noted that the agency also opted against trying to quantify the fare compliance benefits at non-gated stations nor the side benefits they hope to achieve – such as lower maintenance costs due to less vandalism – in their financial calculations, although peer agencies, like BART, have reported such benefits after implementing fare gates. If such benefits do come to pass, the financial boost from fare gates could be even larger, he said.

Without factoring in those potential benefits, the agency estimates gates would still boost fare revenue by at least $30 million annually, an increase of more than 30% compared to today's fare revenue across the entire Sound Transit system.

While a nice little boost, that level of revenue is not likely to be large enough to be a major factor in solving the agency's multi-billion-dollar budget gap through 2046. Once estimated at $34.5 billion, the board reduced its long-term budget gap to about $10 billion in May by delaying or tabling a number of expansion projects – and planning to sunset the Sounder N Line commuter rail service. Every little bit helps, though, fare gate supporters have posited.

The fare gate pilot program received a recommendation from the Rider Experience and Operations Committee earlier this month , generating a more in-depth policy discussion at that juncture. King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci noted the agency would need to set its metrics of success for the program, which she painted as a bit squishy so far.

Some boardmembers also raised equity concerns, about potentially making it harder for low-income residents to access the light rail system. King County Executive Girmay Zahilay highlighted those concerns on Thursday, with de Place noting staff was hoping to ramp up participation in the Orca LIFT reduced fare program.

"Brian, just to clarify, you're saying that between now and when fare gates are installed in the next couple of years, we have a specific plan to set up structures or staffing where people can enroll on site for free and reduced fare cards," Zahilay said. "Is that right?"
De Place said yes, with board authorization.

As it stands, staff said about 91,000 people are enrolled in a reduced fare program. Given the Seattle metropolitan area has a population around 4 million, that suggests a fraction of the people eligible are actually enrolled in ORCA Lift or other reduced fare card programs.
In his report to the board on Thursday, Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine pledged efforts to increase rider awareness as the roll out of the fare gate program approaches.

"Staff have heard loud and clear the emphasis on a thorough and equitable engagement strategy that ensures appropriate fare media and rider awareness materials are available to all passengers once the program is implemented," Constantine said. "Should the board adopt the pilot today, we look forward to keeping you apprised of our progress in tandem with standard design and construction updates you should expect."

After King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda raised a question about access for people with disabilities or with bikes in tow, Sound Transit staff assured the board the agency's Request for Proposal would factor in those needs, and that solutions existed.

"As we move into preparing the RFP and actually coming up with the design of these gates, we'll be working really closely with both the ADA community and the bike community in order to understand the specific needs of those communities vis-a-vis gates," said Meg Cederoth, who is deputy chief planning officer at Sound Transit. "And there are multiple systems in the U.S. where the ADA question has been resolved quite comfortably. We'll be making sure we're engaging with our local communities to understand any unique needs here, and then the bike community as well will be working with them to understand that the gates are wide enough."

Another aspect still to be determined is if the fare gates will be rolled out simultaneously at all 14 proposed stations, or on a rolling basis to test the program more incrementally. The board will still need to greenlight the construction funding before the pilot can fully advance.

articles.title: Op-Ed: From the Bargaining Table to Olympia, Educators Need Our Support Now
articles.author: Kelabe Tewolde
paras: It’s the last few weeks of the summer. Everyone is trying to fit in one last trip out of town, hosting cookouts, spending evenings at the lake, or like many parents diving into back to school shopping. Usually educators are gearing up and preparing to welcome back students to the classroom, but this year there is a bit of a road block.

Between now and September 2nd, the first day of school, members of Seattle Education Association (SEA) are bargaining from 9am to 9pm with Seattle Public Schools (SPS) for a fair contract. That was until last night (August 29th), when SPS walked away from the bargaining table as talks broke down regarding cuts to special education.

On August 26th, SEA authorized a strike. This doesn’t necessarily mean they will strike, but SEA’s bargaining team has the greenlight. With the district walking away from the bargaining table it is increasingly likely SEA will have their third strike in 11 years. We are just a few days away from the start of the school year, and you may be asking, “What’s the hold up?”

SEA has agreed to 12 of 57 issues and struggle to find common ground on what holds the most weight in these negotiations, centering the experience of their students and members. They have found that pressurization and wages are where the district and SEA are unable to come to an agreement. You may be wondering, what this actually means. Teachers are focused on pressurization, a.k.a. increased workload. Pressurization comes in the forms of increases in caseload, class size, and other demands that take their time and focus away from students and lead to educator burnout.

When we constantly put more and more on our educators' plates, we limit the time and energy they have to actually teach our children. And when we talk about wages, we mean making sure all SPS employees can afford to live in the city where they work. In a city as expensive as Seattle, many of the lower-paid workers are finding it difficult to afford to live here in the communities they serve. Educators are not looking for a massive raise in this contract. It is simply a cost-of-living adjustment that will ease the burden of affordability.
If I were to simplify that for the everyday person not at the bargaining table: Teachers want to improve working conditions because their working conditions are their students' learning conditions.
SEA is digging into the district’s annual $1.3 billion budget and finding that part of the problem is state funding. And part of the problem is misplaced priorities.
What is SEA fighting for beyond pressurization and wages?

Special education students have a civil right to a high-quality education : That means we need to meet their individual education plan (IEP). With more students with IEPs in general education, SPS needs to ensure that the co-teaching models are effective. Teachers need an opportunity and space in their schedule to collaborate and help ALL of their students succeed. In these co-teaching models, SPS needs to have a plan to fill in for vacancies and leaves so students with IEPs have teachers with a Special Education endorsement. This is not only an issue around providing a high quality education for all our students, but it is a civil rights issue.

Reasonable class sizes: This is critical to how students succeed. Currently, SEA’s contract includes overage pay as an incentive for the district to keep class sizes a reasonable size, but we are hearing from educators that they don’t want that overage pay. On a personal note, my friend that teaches in a different district similarly had overage pay for having a large class. Mid-year, she had to advocate to split the class up because the learning environment in a class of 35 students was not conducive to student success.

Smaller class sizes give educators the ability to connect with students and help them succeed. SEA states: “We need to create a true cap, beyond which the district must add staff or reduce the class size to ensure students have the opportunity to learn.”
Beyond class sizes, SEA has a variety of other proposals that include safety, AI usage in the classroom, and substitute reimbursement.
Long term, we need solutions from the state
These issues could be solved at the state level if we had a legislature that would prioritize the learning conditions of our children.

In 2014, we had the opportunity to implement smaller class sizes through I-1351 , providing students with one-on-one attention from caring and qualified teachers and support staff. While voters backed smaller class sizes, the state legislature unfortunately left the initiative unfunded, and in 2015 the state legislature delayed its implementation. Eventually in 2017, the legislature repealed the cap on class sizes, due to a lack of funding, leading us to the mess we are in now: Large class sizes, teachers without the resources to effectively serve their students, and students failed by a system that they simply inherited.

Teachers are burnt out and it reflects in how many educators are leaving our schools. One special education teacher told me that: “Last year was the worst teacher year of my life due to an unsustainable and unsupported SpEd caseload. And every SpEd teacher in my building except one left at the end of last year. It’s leading to massive burnout and attrition.”
Without proper class sizes and support, we are failing our teachers, and in turn failing our children.
Many critics to this solution will bring up, “if smaller class sizes were unfunded in 2014, how would you fund them now, especially with an upcoming austerity budget?”

Well, simply put, we would need to reform our tax code like WEA recommended about a decade ago. I’m writing this off the heels of Washington State coming in as No. 1 — for corporate tax breaks and corporations like Microsoft paying a tax rate of 2.4%, while people that earn less than $33,500 a year have a tax rate of 13.8% . We need a legislature that is bold enough to stand up for our values and provide a quality education for all, while creating a sensible tax code that makes everyone pay their fair share .

And this November, we have a choice in legislative races all over the state. We need to elect legislators that are willing to balance the tax code. We deserve legislators who will stand with workers over corporate profits. And legislators that support our educators all year long, not just during an election year.

In the upcoming days, I ask you to support our teachers. This could be showing up for the bargaining team at rallies, spreading the word via social media, calling on the district to meet SEA’s proposals , and, if there is a strike, picketing with teachers throughout the city demanding SPS meet their proposals.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
